title: This Cajun spot on Potrero Hill makes some of the best Southern food in the Bay - NewsBreak
text:
5 hours ago Just off of the main drag of 18th on San Francisco’s Potrero Hill, Poboys Kitchen tells a story of resilience, reinvention, and unexpected opportunity. For more than a decade, chef Metin Yalcin and his brother ran Pera , a beloved Greek restaurant in the city. Their fine-dining approach to Mediterranean flavors won them loyal guests, but when the pandemic struck in 2020, the immense strain of keeping a sit-down restaurant afloat forced them to close its doors.
Photo by A.C. Antonelli What could have been the end of a chapter became the start of something new. Around the same time, part of Metin’s family had moved to Louisiana, just outside New Orleans. That relocation opened a window into the world of Southern cuisine—Cajun and Creole in particular. At first, it was curiosity that drove him. Trained as a chef and rooted in Kurdish-American heritage, Metin began studying these traditions from a cultural and historical perspective. But quickly, passion overtook study. He trained, cooked, and immersed himself in Louisiana kitchens, never imagining this would one day inspire a restaurant of his own.
Photo by Po'Boys Kitchen The idea for Poboys Kitchen came almost by accident. When friends in Louisiana and San Francisco tasted his spin on Cajun and Creole classics, they urged him to share them more widely. One of those tastings even convinced his current landlord to offer him a space. In October 2020—without fanfare, without walk-in traffic, and with the world still shuttered—Poboys Kitchen opened its doors for takeout only. The timing was daunting, but word of mouth carried quickly through Potrero Hill. Longtime fans of Metin’s Greek cooking, combined with curious locals, gave the fledgling restaurant a chance. Then came the turning point: San Francisco Chronicle food columnist Justin Phillips wrote about the restaurant, shining a citywide spotlight on the chef’s Cajun-Creole debut.
The name itself reflects the dual identity of the venture. The po’boy sandwich is an icon of New Orleans cuisine, but the name also nods to “PO,” short for Potrero Hill, grounding the restaurant firmly in its San Francisco home. It’s a fitting reflection of Metin’s cooking: Southern at its heart, but filtered through the lens of a chef who brings both Mediterranean training and cross-cultural perspective to the table.
Photo by Po'Boys Kitchen At Poboys Kitchen, the menu bridges authenticity with creativity. Classics like shrimp & grits, seafood jambalaya, and fried chicken topped with popcorn sit alongside the restaurant’s namesake po’boys, layered with bold flavors and a touch of personality. The combination draws a diverse clientele—locals, visitors, and even a few high-profile names. Over the years, Metin has welcomed actors Danny Glover and Craig Robinson, musician Carlos Santana, Metallica bassist Robert Trujillo, Spanish actress Úrsula Corberó, and even former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair. NBA teams, too, have made Poboys a dining stop when traveling through San Francisco.
Yet the restaurant’s greatest success lies not in its celebrity clientele but in the everyday connections formed across the counter. For Metin, the best part of running Poboys Kitchen is watching guests take their first bite. Often, he says, there’s hesitation—Southerners wondering if a Bay Area chef could truly honor their deeply rooted traditions. Then comes the surprise, and finally the smile. “That moment,” he reflects, “is the best motivation I could ask for.”
Photo by Po'Boys Kitchen Operating any independent restaurant in San Francisco comes with steep challenges. Rising rents, food costs, and staffing shortages press on daily operations. For Southern cuisine, the challenge doubles: diners often carry deeply personal expectations tied to their family recipes. Meeting those expectations, while adding his own signature, is no easy feat. But the warm support of Potrero Hill neighbors and the dedication of his team have carried Poboys Kitchen forward.
Now in its fifth year, the restaurant continues to grow not by expanding locations or chasing trends, but by deepening its ties to the community. Metin’s vision is simple: to keep cooking the food he loves, supporting his staff, and serving the guests who’ve embraced this unlikely Cajun-Creole home in San Francisco.
Poboys Kitchen
📍 317 Connecticut St, San Francisco, CA 94107
🍴 Established: October 16, 2020
👨‍🍳 Chef-Owner: Metin Yalcin
🥖 Concept: Cajun & Creole flavors through the eyes of a Kurdish-American chef, rooted in Potrero Hill
⭐ Signature Dishes: Po’boys, Shrimp & Grits, Seafood Jambalaya, Popcorn-Topped Fried Chicken
Opening Hours
Sun - Thurs: 11a to 8p
Fri - Sat: 11a to 9p 9
